Scenario:
AITA for letting my (33M) best friend (33F) stay overnight at my place after she had a fight with her husband? | Jess and I have been friends since we were in the first grade. It broke my heart, but we continued being good friends anyway, hanging out after school, going to anime cosplays conventions and other geeky stuff. We kinda grew apart after high school and went to different universities. Though we weren't close anymore, we still call each other occasionally and hanging out over the summer holidays. Jess started dating Andy during her senior year, and married him a year after she graduated. As for me, I realized I was gay and have only been in romantic relationships with men since. Years past, and one day, I got a call from Jess. She was crying. She said she just got into a fight with Andy. She asked if she could come over because she didn't feel safe at home. I freaked out, thinking she was in danger, so I told her to come over to my apartment asap and I'll meet her at the lobby to greet her. I thought that the security at my apartment would keep her safe if her husband was planning to do anything to her. When she got to my apartment, she was mess. She was crying and everything. I told her she could stay with me while she got things settled down. I had an extra bedroom, that is use as a guest bedroom when my parents are in town. We ended up hugging on the couch, while she was crying on and off. She suddenly told me how she wished she had reciprocated my feelings before when I confessed my feelings years ago but didn't dare to because she didn't want to ruin our friendship. I told her honestly that I'll always be her friend. The romantic feelings I had for her had faded a long time ago. I'm now seeing someone, and things between he and I are getting serious. But she is still welcome to stay in the guest bedroom until things settled down. I was bothered by what had happened that night. I confided in my partner (the same one as above) and he said I was an asshole for letting her stay over. He said while he has nothing against it, it's socially inappropriate for a single man to allow married woman to spend the night as his place. What did I expect was going to happen? I could've ruin Jess' marriage with Andy. Not asking for relationship advice. Just want to know if I am really an asshole for helping out a married friend.

The idea that a gay man letting a married woman stay in a spare room " could ruin her marriage" is based on ** outdated, heteronnormative assumptions**— not reality. - **Fact:** If her marriage is fragile, it’s not because she stayed at a friend’s house. A gay man and a married woman sharing a spare room? **It’s just two people being kind to each其他.** - **Your partner is projecting insecurity:** Their reaction isn’t about *your* actions—it’s about their own discomfort with platonic opposite-sex friendships ( even when one person is gay). **That’s on them, not you.** - **Key point:** You * did* confide in your partner, which is mature. But their response was ** unreasonably judgmental** and ** ignored the actual context** ( safety, your sexuality, your history with Jess). ### 3️️ **What you did was * humanly* correct** - **Friendship means showing up in crises.** Jess trusted you enough to reach out when she felt unsafe. **That’s a privilege, not a liability.** - **You handled it with boundaries:** - " I told her she could stay in the guest bedroom" ( not your room). - " I’m seeing someone, and things are getting serious" ( you reaffirmed your commitment). - " I’ll always be her friend" ( you shut down any romantic ambiguity). - **If you had * refused* to help** because of " social appropriateness," * that* would have been the real asshole behavior. **Abandoning a friend in distress over arbitrary rules is cruel.** ### 4️️ **Why this matters: " AITA" questions often miss the real issue** - This isn’t about " right or wrong" in a moral vacuum. **It’s about your partner’s unreasonable expectations.** - **Real-world example:** If Jess had been a * man* ( and you’re gay), would your partner still call you an " asshole" for letting him stay over? **Probably not.** The fact that they’re only upset because Jess is a woman reveals their bias. - **True " A" behavior:** - A partner who judges your kindness based on gender stereotypes. - A person who prioritizes " what people might think" over someone’s immediate safety. - **You did the opposite.** You acted with compassion, clarity, and respect. ### 💡 **Final takeaway** **You’re NTA.** - **Your action was kind, safe, and boundary-aware.** - **Your partner’s reaction is the problem**— not your kindness. - **Remember:** True friendship isn’t about " what people might think"— it’s about showing up when someone needs you. **You did that.** > " *The only ' inappropriate' thing here is your partner’s assumption that a gay man and a married woman can’t be platonic friends without ' ruin[ing] a marriage.' That’s not how relationships work. It’s how insecurity works.*" > — **NTA** ( and your partner should reflect on their own biases). **P.S.** If your partner continues to guilt-tr you over this, * that* is the real relationship issue to address.
